I7IAutomatic calibration: the search algorithm and its evaluation budgetPARTIALcalibrate.py:163 rebuild_stage admits matsim_param bindings (movable set 21), :561 CAL.search.points_per_parameter, :725 evaluate re-assembles per candidate; --execute refuses while within-run drift exceeds the band; never completed a candidate.Every deviation; the loop has no finished evaluation to its name.Calibrating a microsimulation is a black-box, stochastic, expensive simulation-based optimisation problem, and the published methods separate by how many simulation evaluations they can afford. SPSA (simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation) is the field's workhorse because it costs only two simulation evaluations per gradient estimate whatever the dimension, and W-SPSA extends it with a weight matrix; but it is built for asymptotic guarantees rather than early termination, and under a small budget it barely moves - on a Salt Lake City origin-destination calibration of order thirty thousand dimensions SPSA took the vehicle-count nRMSE from 120% to 117% over fifteen simulation iterations, while a metamodel method reached 32%. Evolutionary strategies (CMA-ES, xNES) and finite-difference gradient approximation (FDSA, SPSA) are what the MATSim/eqasim calibration framework boptx implements. The cross-entropy method is a Monte-Carlo importance-sampling search and is the most expensive family: one published SUMO calibration of a three-intersection model spent 98,304 simulation evaluations. Bayesian optimisation over a surrogate is the current answer for a small budget (see the surrogate row). The field states its own constraint plainly: computational budgets in the literature are 'one to two orders of magnitude lower than the problem dimension', and general-purpose algorithms 'are designed for asymptotic performance guarantees and are not designed to be terminated with such few function evaluations'.https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.113922026-09-08
I8ISurrogate / metamodel-assisted calibrationOUTNo surrogate anywhere in src/calibrate (grep 'surrogate|metamodel|gaussian process|kriging': none).None; 25 % arms cost 39-50 h each (K2), which is where a surrogate would pay.The canonical line is Osorio's metamodel simulation-based optimisation: replace the expensive simulated objective with an analytical network model plus a low-order statistical correction, then solve a sequence of cheap analytical problems, so that good points are found from the first iterations without a large initial sample. Its strongest published demonstration is a Salt Lake City origin-destination calibration of order thirty thousand dimensions, where within ONE simulation iteration the linear-metamodel method took the vehicle-count nRMSE from 120% to 32%, against 48% for a tailored linear-assignment method and 117% for SPSA, all inside a fifteen-simulation-iteration budget - and 'thereafter there is not much improvement within such few iterations', i.e. nearly all the gain arrives at the first evaluation. The second family is machine-learned rather than analytical: a random-forest surrogate driving Bayesian optimisation calibrated 477 behavioural parameters of the SimMobility MT activity-based model for Tallinn, and did so against AGGREGATE benchmarks ('the modal share of the whole population'), reaching 4% error on the total number of trips and an average origin-destination error of 15.92 vehicles per day. That paper states no prior work had calibrated as many as 477 parameters and that existing rigorous methods 'do not consider more than a few dozen of parameters (the maximum number being 98)'.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.034802026-09-08
I9IIdentifiability under many simultaneous targetsPARTIALCAL.objective.independent_targets = 10 (calibrate.py:483, :560) records the folds; the objective is a max over twelve modes; no identifiability test is computed.taxi and bike share one HTS 'Other' cell, so one of the two deviations is not independent evidence.A parameter set is identified only if distinct parameter values produce distinguishable outputs on the targets you actually hold, and the simulation-calibration literature is explicit that when a model is over-parametrised relative to its targets, 'non-identifiability can arise, making it theoretically impossible to locate the true parameter value'. The published remedy is not a better optimiser but a different answer: report an ELIGIBILITY SET - the set of all parameter values whose simulated outputs match the data - constructed to carry rigorous frequentist guarantees, extended to multivariate outputs by a feature-extraction-then-aggregation construction. The counting rule underneath is what binds a mode-share calibration: K shares that sum to one contain K-1 independent numbers, so scoring twelve modelled modes against a five-mode survey does not supply twelve independent targets. The only way to buy identifiability for more parameters is to add targets of a DIFFERENT kind - link counts, boardings, trip-length and duration distributions - not more shares of the same total. The OD-calibration literature reaches the same place from the other side: 'the problem is underdetermined ... there are typically an infinite number of vectors x that can reproduce these counts', which is why a regularisation term toward a prior seed matrix is standard.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2105.128932026-09-08

(1) AGGREGATE ASC ADJUSTMENT, the practice standard: iteratively add the log ratio of observed to modelled share to each mode constant, re-run, repeat until the split is inside a stated threshold, commonly plus or minus one percentage point; ActivitySim adjusts tour-level and trip-level constants together with the same increment because tour mode conditions trip mode. The profession's own validation manual warns that revising constants is 'a last resort' after other checks are exhausted, because a constant absorbs every omitted variable. (2) BLP-STYLE DEMAND INVERSION: a contraction mapping inverts observed market shares to implied mean utilities and GMM on instrumented moments recovers heterogeneous taste coefficients 'from only aggregate market-share data', removing the IIA restriction on substitution; the requirement is instruments with genuine cross-market variation, which a single-city model does not naturally possess. (3) SURROGATE-ASSISTED SIMULATION-BASED ESTIMATION against aggregate benchmarks: the Tallinn SimMobility work fitted 477 behavioural parameters entirely against 'aggregate benchmarks (e.g., the modal share of the whole population)' and names disaggregate data only as future work - a direct feasibility proof that unit records are not a precondition for fitting a large behavioural parameter set.https://tfresource.org/topics/Model_Validation_and_Reasonableness_Checking_Mode_Choice.html2026-09-08

K3KReproducibility of a runPARTIALSeeded everywhere (RUN.machine.seed, B.seed.master; TreeMap draw order since 9.151); controler, inputs and values sha256 recorded per run (run_matsim.py:106, :956, :976); MATSim itself is not bit-reproducible across runs of one build (three runs disagree from iteration 2) and no replication band exists (I4).As I4.Run-to-run reproducibility is not achievable by fixing a seed alone in this class of model: across 100 seeds relative errors up to 10% occur on high-volume links, and between-seed variation dominates the last-two-iteration within-seed variation. I11ISequential versus simultaneous calibration of many targetsINThe objective is the MAX over all twelve modes at once (CAL.objective.components goal_modes.max_abs_rel_pct; calibrate.py:288 objective, :469 components); the ASC loop moves all constants in one round.None specific.The field states the choice explicitly and it is a real fork, not a matter of taste. In dynamic OD calibration, 'the first formulation estimates the whole set of time-dependent OD matrices SIMULTANEOUSLY for the entire time period in one calibration round. The second formulation estimates and calibrates OD matrices SEQUENTIALLY one at a time for each time frame. Most optimization-based studies have used the simultaneous approach, since the available sequential methods may lose accuracy due to giving up some information in the transition between time frames' - while the simultaneous form 'is incapable of handling a stream of data for real-time or online demand calibration'. The same paper states the bind that makes the choice matter at all: 'this optimization problem is underdetermined for large-scale networks since the number of roads with traffic measurement is usually several orders of magnitude smaller than the number of all roads in the network', and it names the standard architecture as BI-LEVEL - an upper-level discrepancy minimisation over an inner assignment that must be re-solved at every candidate, where 'performing several DTAs for each optimization task demand considerable computational resources'. In DTA practice the sequential form is supply first and then demand with the supply held fixed; the reported weakness of decomposing is that the stages need not be internally consistent, because each stage's assumed input is not the other stage's output.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.173152026-09-09
I12IDamping and step-size schedule in the constant-adjustment contractionINCAL.asc.damping 0.6 is a fixed fraction and CAL.asc.max_step_utils 1.5 a refusal bound (asc_fixed_point.py:19-26, :111-112); no schedule. This pass read the reference implementation (matsim-python-tools calc_asc_update): the raw log-ratio with NO damping and lr defaulting to None - the 0.6 is this project's own.Nothing until the loop runs.The log-ratio ASC step is a contraction only if it is damped, and the two open implementations of it disagree on how. The leading open MATSim calibrator, matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools, computes the raw step verbatim as 'math.log(z_i) - math.log(m_i) - (math.log(z_0) - math.log(m_0))' and applies it under a SCHEDULE whose default is 'linear_scheduler(start=0.6, end=1, interval=3)' - the early rounds take 0.6 of the raw step and the fraction relaxes to the full step over three intervals, i.e. cautious while the shares are far from target and undamped once they are near. The agency practice in the ActivitySim world applies a FLAT dampener instead of a schedule. Neither publishes a convergence proof, and the same library's 'TerminationCondition.check_termination' still carries '# TODO: not used yet' - so the field's standard answer ships a damping default and no working stopping rule at all. The undamped step (1.0) is the boundary case: it is what a fixed point converges to when it converges, and what overshoots when the shares are far out.https://github.com/matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools/blob/master/matsim/calibration/utils.py2026-09-09

Three modes classified: ride = choice set; bike, taxi = constant-reachable.ride -41.0 is diagnosed mechanism; taxi +202.2 and bike +113.0 constant-movable in the arithmetic sense.The profession's own manual puts constant adjustment LAST and lists what must be exhausted first. FHWA's Travel Model Validation and Reasonableness Checking Manual, chapter 7 (Mode Choice / Vehicle Occupancy), states that 'simple adjustments to modal constants estimated using weighted samples should be considered "a last resort" after all other possible causes for error and calibration adjustments have been considered', and its Table 7.6 orders the checks ahead of it: verify trip distribution for the market segment, check that the implied transit share is reasonable, recheck the skim data (networks, time periods, geographic scope), consider revising the model STRUCTURE, evaluate indicator variables or adjust their coefficients - and only then revise an alternative-specific constant. The same chapter states plainly that 'there are no applicable criteria guidelines for checks of mode choice', so the field supplies an ORDER of diagnosis and no numeric bar. What it does not supply anywhere reached this pass is a TEST that separates the two cases: no source reviewed proposes reading the round-over-round behaviour of the constant update itself as the diagnostic.https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/planning/tmip/publications/other_reports/validation_and_reasonableness_2010/ch07.cfm2026-09-09
I14IMulti-objective aggregation across many simultaneous targetsINMax-over-modes (Chebyshev) objective (calibrate.py:288-323), CAL.objective.components; counts excluded (CAL.objective.include_counts false).As I11.Aggregating many targets into one number has a known and specific failure. Jakob and Blume set it out: with a weighted sum, 'by varying the weights, any point of a convex Pareto front can be obtained... On the other hand, it is possible that parts of the Pareto front cannot be found in case of a non-convex problem... the part between points A and B of the Pareto front cannot be obtained for any weights. This is a serious drawback.' The counterweight is cost: 'the computational effort to determine all or at least most of the Pareto front increases significantly with the number of conflicting objectives', and the paper's framing is that the real-world question arises 'where either more than four objectives have to be considered, or the same type of task is repeated again and again with only minor modifications'. So beyond about four conflicting targets a full Pareto treatment is expensive and scalarisation is the practical route - while the scalarisation chosen decides which compromises are reachable at all. A weighted sum of squared deviations across targets is the standard form in simulation-based transport calibration.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.026972026-09-09
F5FRouter-scorer consistency: does the search optimise the utility the plan is scored by?PARTIALThree consistency mechanisms exist and all ship off: C.raptor.mode_cost_representation = absent (RaptorModeCostCalculator.java:103 caches -modeParams.getConstant() per submode, :112 getInVehicleCost); RUN.mode_choice.pt_submode_alternatives = aggregate (SubmodeRaptorProvider.java:66, one raptor per submode over a filtered schedule; PtSubmodeChoiceConfigGroup CitysimControler.java:240); C.time_weights.service_quality_representation = absent. What DID move: the router's access/egress/transfer walks are now the network legs the mobsim executes (NetworkDirectWalkPtRouter bound :328-331; 5de5080), closing the router-mobsim inconsistency of 9.159. Proof of the remaining inconsistency: 0.63 % of agents hold plans differing in pt submode (9.160).light_rail -58.6 / heavy_rail +225.0 / bus +44.8 / ferry -60.1 are ALL decided in the layer with no control; any one switch opens a family.MATSim's own choice-model chapter makes the split explicit: an agent's realised behaviour is P(i|U) = sum over choice sets of P(i|C) x P(C|U) - the choice model AND the way the choice set was generated. The router is the choice-set generator, so a router that optimises a different objective from the scoring function generates alternatives the scorer will then reject, and 'alternatives that never appear in the choice set cannot be chosen'. MATSim's stock car routing keeps the two aligned by deriving the link travel cost from the scoring parameters (the negative marginal utility of travelling plus the marginal utility of performing); the alignment is deliberate and is broken wherever a specialised router is used. The SwissRailRaptor's DefaultRaptorInVehicleCostCalculator prices a boarded leg as in-vehicle seconds times one coefficient, so a per-submode constant, a fare or a crowding surcharge that lives only in scoring is invisible to the transit search that picks the submode.https://d-nb.info/1172809151/342026-09-10
H9HEquilibrium selection and the innovation cutoff: what the reported share is a share OFPARTIALThe cutoff's effect is MEASURED per mode (summarise_run.py:156-169 snap_pp, cutoff_to_final_pp; car +2.211, walk -0.941, ride -0.489, taxi -0.583) and two estimator controls are DECLARED and unrun: RUN.replanning.score_msa_representation (absent | at_innovation_cutoff) and RUN.replanning.plan_selector_for_removal (sweep over MATSim's five); a warm-started arm re-derives the cutoff so it stays the parent's iteration (a50e9c7, #192).car +11.3 was inside the band before the cutoff; walk left the band through it. Which share is validated is still a decision.MATSim's iterative loop is not stationary while innovation runs: its own terminology page states that 'as long as innovation is still switched on in MATSim (new routes, new times, ...), the result is not truly stationary', and that once innovation is disabled 'the result is indeed a stationary process, but limited to the set of plans that every agent has at that point in time'. The selection protocol before the cutoff 'resembles a MNL choice model', P(i|C) = exp(mu S_i)/sum exp(mu S_j) with mu = brainExpBeta, and the chapter notes that BestPlanSelector is the same selector with an infinite mu. So the pre-cutoff share is a logit-dispersed mixture over each agent's remembered plans and the post-cutoff share is the same population collapsed toward its arg-max: switching innovation off changes the estimator, not only the amount of search. Assignment theory says the same thing from the other side - a low dispersion parameter concentrates flow on the perceived-best alternative and the pattern approaches deterministic user equilibrium, which is the classic 'unrealistic route concentration' that stochastic user equilibrium was introduced to cure. The efficiency loss of that concentration is bounded and modest on real networks - a data-driven estimate for Eastern Massachusetts puts the price of anarchy near 1.30, and other empirical work finds it close to 1 in both light and heavy traffic - so an equilibrium being reached is no guarantee that it resembles the observed day, which is itself a non-equilibrium average.https://matsim.org/docs/userguide/terminology.html2026-09-10
H10HChoice-set coverage as a binding constraint on any constant or priceINsrc/analyse/report_choice_set_coverage.py reads modeChoiceCoverage1x.txt (:88), prints headroom = coverage - share per mode and classifies a deviation larger than its headroom as a choice-set finding (:231 _reachable); report_mode_ridership.py:678-707 prints the unreachable list on every board reading; truck/motorbike refused a headroom, boardings-basis modes not compared.ride -41.0 (target 20.60 above coverage 20.05) is the one deviation the gate names as unreachable by any constant; pt 25.78 % bounds the four pt submodes together.Flotterod and Kickhofer state the mechanism in one line and it is an identity, not a tendency: 'the generation of the choice sets affects the simulated choices. The simplest illustration of this mechanism is that alternatives that never appear in the choice set cannot be chosen. Similarly, including certain alternatives with a low (high) probability in the choice set decreases (increases) their probability of being chosen, given that the choice model is not changed.' They add the consequence for a calibration exercise directly: 'When a choice study's synthetic choice sets are very different from the alternatives considered in the real world, it is unlikely that the simulation will display correct aggregated quantities or useful sensitivities for policy measures', and that MATSim's mutation and innovation procedures 'constitute concrete, yet heuristic, approaches to the choice set generation problem' whose biases 'can, however, be difficult to quantify'. The plan memory is the other half of the constraint: the choice set is bounded by maxAgentPlanMemorySize, plans past it are deleted by a PlanSelectorForRemoval, and the MATSim user guide records that 'a problem is that the process that generates the choice set at this point is not systematic'. A mode constant therefore has an upper bound on what it can move that is set by the fraction of agents who ever held that mode in memory, not by its own magnitude.https://d-nb.info/1172809151/342026-09-10
H11HMode availability by distance: an upper bound on a walk or bike alternativeINERTB.mode.walk_feasible_km and B.mode.bike_feasible_km are declared (derived 3.22 / 23.95 km), bound (matsim_param modeAvailability.walkFeasibleKm), reach GatedSubtourModeChoice.java:228 beyondReach (:472) and SHIP AT 0.0 where the consumer returns false - check_hardcoding section 7 at this HEAD lists both as 'shipped at the consumer's off value' (inert_at 0.0).bike +113.0 with 7.32 km mean against 5.2: the cap at its derived p99 made the fit worse (9.106) and is refused.Cycling distance is short and its distribution is well measured. Australian travel survey data for 2012-2020 put the median home-based cycling trip at 3.5 km, varying strongly by purpose - 1.8 km utilitarian, 5.3 km commuting, 3.7 km recreational - with trip purpose the strongest predictor and men cycling further than women. The Montreal metropolitan survey puts the 85th percentile of cycling distance at 5,517 m, and the 85th-percentile access distance is the field's usual way of setting a catchment. Distance decay for cycling fits an exponential or lognormal curve rather than a cliff, so the correct representation is a decaying utility rather than a hard cut-off - but a simulator that offers the mode at any distance with no decay term places mass far out in a tail the survey does not contain.https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11675929/2026-09-10
I15IDistributional targets beyond mode share: trip length, intrazonal share, occupancyPARTIALfit.py:416 score_occupancy and :437 score_trip_geometry compute occupancy and mean length/time per mode and declare them constraints (C.constraint.*), not fit components; no trip-length distribution or intrazonal share target; the bespoke trip-length-by-mode table is drafted (J7).walk mean 3.28 km vs 0.70, bike 7.32 vs 5.2, ride occupancy 0.186 vs 0.3503: the geometry says where the shares are wrong and is not optimised against.The profession does not accept a mode share as a model's validation on its own; it validates the distribution the share is drawn from. The standing guidance is explicit and numeric: 'Generally, the modeled average trip lengths for each trip purpose should be within five percent of observed for each trip purpose'; the trip length frequency distribution is compared as a whole using the coincidence ratio - 'the area under both curves divided by the area under at least one of the curves' - and 'it is preferable for the coincidence ratio for each trip purpose to be at least 70 percent'; and 'regionwide intrazonal trip percentages should be within three percentage points of observed for each trip purpose'. Vehicle occupancy has moved into the same class: in trip-based models the vehicle occupancy factor was an input converting person trips to vehicle trips, while 'in activity-based models (ABM), the role of VOF transitioned from a major input to a validation target for shared-rides'. On the assignment side the same manuals give volume tolerances by facility class - Ohio's VMT guidance is plus or minus 7 per cent on freeways and expressways, 10 per cent on principal and minor arterials, 15 per cent on collectors, with Michigan DOT at 5 and 10 per cent for screenlines and cutlines and Florida at 20 per cent for transit screenlines - while stating that 'the guidelines in this section should not be construed as standards'.https://tfresource.org/topics/Model_Validation_and_Reasonableness_Checking_Distribution.html2026-09-10
K4KFlow-capacity, storage-capacity and stuck-time correction at a sample fractionPARTIALRUN.sample.flow_capacity_factor derived = fraction, storage exponent 1.0 (alpha = 1), RUN.qsim.stuck_time_s 10 (RUN_execution.json:1272-1284, assumed, sweep [10, 600]); the taxi fleet and SCATS saturation flow scale by the flow factor; no scaled stuck time. The literature now states the rule (this pass): stuckTime = 30 s / share, i.e. 120 s at 25 %, inside the declared sweep and unrun.car stuck 3,786 at F30 iteration 0; RUN.qsim.stuck_time_s at 120 is the literature's value for this fraction and opens a family.The correction rules for a downscaled run are contested and were measured again this year. Mersini and Ziemke (MUM 2025, TU Berlin) set out the position: former recommendations scaled storage less than flow, flowCapacityFactor = sample share and storageCapacityFactor = sample share^alpha with alpha = 0.75 'to prevent breakdowns in small samples', while 'more recently, flow and storage capacities are usually scaled equally, i.e., with alpha = 1', the Open Berlin practice; Llorca and Moeckel found 'no substantial differences in average travel times for a given MATSim scenario when comparing different sample shares using both alpha values', and Ben-Dor, Ben-Elia and Benenson again recommend 0.75. Their measured result on a 100 per cent Lausitz benchmark is that scores and travel times are close to the full-scale run at 25 and 50 per cent, deviate at 5 per cent and clearly at 1 per cent, and that 'even average statistics (such as score and travel time) become unreliable when sampling below 10%'. The sharper finding is on the third parameter nobody scales: stuck-time violations, normalised by the inverse sample share, rise from about 40,000 at 100 per cent (about one agent in eight stuck once per day) to three times as many at 1 per cent, and with equal scaling of flow and storage 'even more than four and a half times as many' - so alpha = 1 costs stuck agents at small samples, and the paper flags that stuck time itself should be scaled with the sample size, larger for smaller samples.https://matsim.org/conferences/mum2025/abstracts/MUM25_paper_30.pdf2026-09-10
K5KExpanding a sampled run's link volumes for a counts comparisonPARTIAL1/fraction expansion applied (src/analyse/extract_metrics.py:21-28); station-to-link matching repaired and re-cut on the footpath network (202 stations); the light-vehicle conversion still runs on an ASSUMED heavy share at the unclassified stations (:616, B.counts.heavy_vehicle_share 0.0652); B.counts.vehicles_per_car_leg / per_ride_leg still declared ahead of consumer (#20).counts +16.3 %: half of the basis is measured; the vehicle-per-leg conversion and the heavy share at 27 of 30 stations are the assumed half.A downscaled run's link volumes must be multiplied back before they mean anything against an observed count, and MATSim carries the factor as a first-class setting: countsScaleFactor 'represents a multiplier for scaling model results back to real-world volumes, so that when a model is based on a countsScaleFactor of 10, the real fleet sizes would be ten times higher'. The expansion is only the first of three basis decisions, and the other two are where practice models put their error bars: WHICH simulated vehicles count (the observed detector counts every vehicle class, so the modelled side must either add its heavy vehicles or the observed side must be converted to a light-vehicle basis - one or the other, never neither), and WHICH link a station maps to (a two-way station is the sum of both directions and a station matched to a service road or the wrong carriageway reads near zero). The tolerance guidance is by volume class rather than per link, and the manuals warn against reading it as a standard: 'the guidelines in this section should not be construed as standards; matching or exceeding the guidelines is not sufficient to determine the validity of a model.'https://tfresource.org/topics/Model_Validation_and_Reasonableness_Checking_Assignment.html2026-09-10

Currie and Delbosc's BRT/LRT comparison attributes part of the gap to load factor, reliability, comfort and visibility, and part to perception. TfNSW publishes BOAM (Bus Opal Assignment Model), 'an indicator of historic bus occupancy for individual bus services from January 2020' under Creative Commons Attribution, with a v2.0 field document behind login; its regional coverage is not stated on the page. Every Hunter and Lower North Coast bus has been fitted with GPS and automatic passenger counting under the Transport Connected Bus programme (233 buses), and PTIPS-based on-time running is published for Sydney Metropolitan and Outer Metropolitan contracts from 2010. GTFS-Realtime for the Hunter is live and can be archived by the user.https://opendata.transport.nsw.gov.au/dataset/boam-bus-opal-assignment-model2026-09-11
J7JBespoke aggregate tables from the travel survey where unit records are not releasedOUTNo bespoke HTS cross-tabulation has been received. The request for four cells is DRAFTED at cities/newcastle/docs/requests/tfnsw_hts_bespoke_tables.md (b8f6577; the hub's CKAN API searched and found none of them) and NOT SENT - sending is the operator's act. transport.nsw.gov.au returned 403 again this pass.bike +113.0 (12-17 year olds at 15.4 %) and taxi's age gate: the observed mode x age cell is one bespoke table away.TfNSW publishes the Household Travel Survey by Region, LGA and SA3 (2020/21-2024/25 released 9 March 2026; dashboards) and states that to protect respondents it is 'unable to provide the data in any alternative form or at a more granular level'; the same programme supplies BESPOKE tables - the dataset page says 'If you have been supplied bespoke journey data for historical years recently, please request updated tables' (contact opendataprogram@transport.nsw.gov.au). A model that cannot estimate on unit records can still request the specific cross-tabulation its target needs (mode by age band, trip-length distribution by mode, occupancy by purpose) for its study area.https://opendata.transport.nsw.gov.au/dataset/household-travel-survey2026-09-11
E26ECar: per-kilometre operating cost, congestion time, chain-based availabilityINNEW ROW (car). Per-km cost: C.scoring.monetary_distance_rate car -0.00018 AUD/m (derived, matsim_param scoring.modeParams[*].monetaryDistanceRate) times the marginal utility of money, income-scaled (E8); congestion time via the one trip-weighted VOT (C.scoring.marginal_utility_of_traveling derived from C.vot.trip_weighted 16.96); parking price and search time (E4); chain-based availability (RUN.mode_choice.chain_based_modes [car, bike], GatedSubtourModeChoice.java:515) and the household roster (E6, HouseholdCarDepartureHandler); car is a qsim main mode on the congested network with RUN.travel_time.filter_modes true. The perceived-cost finding (fuel-like marginal cost only) is what the per-km rate implements.car +11.3: at the literature's -0.16 short-run car-km elasticity a 10 % change in the per-km cost moves car-km about 1.6 %, so the excess is not a per-km-cost finding; the roster (+2.211 pp car at the cutoff) and the ride placement (F35 arm 0) are where car's +11.3 sits.Car use is price-inelastic in the short run and elastic only over the long run and only with respect to TOTAL cost. The European review by de Jong and Gunn (2001), as tabulated by Litman, gives car-kilometres with respect to fuel price -0.16 short term and -0.26 long term (commuting -0.12 / -0.23), and car-kilometres with respect to travel time -0.20 short term and -0.74 long term; Goodwin (1996) gives urban-road vehicle travel with respect to travel time -0.27 short run and -0.57 long run. Litman's synthesis states the scaling explicitly: a -0.1 short-run elasticity of vehicle travel with respect to fuel price reflects a -0.3 long-run elasticity, which reflects about -1.2 with respect to total vehicle costs, because most vehicle costs (depreciation, financing, insurance, registration, residential parking) are fixed and short-run effects are about a third of long-run ones. Brons, Nijkamp, Pels and Rietveld's meta-analysis of gasoline-demand price elasticities (158 estimates) finds the demand response driven mainly by fuel efficiency and car ownership and to a lesser degree by mileage per car, with a long-run estimate about -0.46 for total fuel demand. On what a driver actually prices, the classic Transportation paper 'Perceived and actual costs of operating cars' finds the modal split consistent with drivers perceiving petrol costs only, which is why mode-choice models price car by a marginal per-kilometre cost rather than by full cost of ownership.https://www.vtpi.org/elasticities.pdf2026-09-14

verdict

followed
Yes, and faster than before: 19 of the 11 Sep report's 20 recommendations are TAKEN (3 of them partial), 1 OPEN, none overtaken or repeated - 95 % against 72 % for R1-R6 - and all of it landed in three PRs within 36 hours (#193 the same night, #194 and #195 the next day). Across the series 126 of 158 recommendations (80 %) are taken, 29 open, 2 overtaken, 1 repeated-only.
moved_the_scoreboard
No. There has been no reading since the 11 Sep report: F33 died, F34 opened on a rebuild with no arm, and F35 arm 0 is running unread (iteration 284 of 300 at 14 Sep 01:22). The newest result is still F32 at 0 of 12 inside; the newest citable gate F31 at 1 of 12. Gates fired since: 0 (25 in the series). What the recommendations moved is requirement 1 (walk on footpaths, pt access legs physical), requirement 6 (three observations acquired) and the launcher (heap rule, stall kill, no-op overlay refused) - and the cost: the footpath network doubled the iteration (244.5 -> 555.5 s), F35 recovered 17 % (460 s quoted, 362.8 s/it measured on arm 0), so a 300-iteration arm is ~30 h again rather than the ~21 h of F32.
what_was_taken
Everything mechanical and one model change: the twenty asks were harness (1, 2, 16, 18, 19), consolidation (6, 7, 8), process (13, 14, 15), documents (10), data (12, 17) and two model-side items (4 plan removal; 20 the footpath network) - the footpath rebuild is the one recommendation in the series that opened a family on its own. The recommendation that keeps not being taken is the one that needs an external party: the TfNSW request has been drafted twice (#177, #194) and sent never.
cadence
Right on the rule and wrong on the hour. The rule since 11 Sep is once per reading - after a gate or horizon, after a family opens on a rebuild, or on request. This pass follows the F34 rebuild and the F35 opening, which the rule allows, but the reading it should follow is 1.6 hours away: arm 0 stood at iteration 284 of 300, 362.8 s/it, not stalled, at 14 Sep 01:22. A report lodged now can only repeat the built-unrun verdict of 11 Sep (score MSA, raptor constant, service quality, submodes, the replication band) and its recommendations about the reading will be superseded by the arm before they are read. The series' own history says what that costs: the 7 Sep trio 4.5 h and 5.7 h apart re-marked 118 of 131 and 104 of 138 findings STILL OPEN. The right pass is the one after 20260912T202242_300it_25pct writes ran_to_last_iteration - or this one, held for it.
this_report
Any re-issue of the rows in still_open_from_last is a repeat: the replication band would be its sixth issue, the TfNSW lodgement its fifth, the raptor-constant control arm its third, the second reviewer its third, the answer sweeps their third.

Recommendations, ranked

Ranked by what each would prevent or move × how cheap it is. A repeat tag marks one an earlier report already issued; the process audit counts them against this report too.

  1. Fix the reader before anything is read again: resolve a run's transit schedule from its own output/output_transitSchedule.xml.gz, then regenerate the board's scoreboard block and the ninth report's rail cells from it.
    The board's only RESULT reads heavy rail 0 / -100 % through a schedule the run never drove (finding 1); arm 0's it.300 reading will be right by accident only because it drove the rebuilt schedule. Every pre-rebuild reading is now unreadable at HEAD.
    change: src/analyse/extract_metrics.py:308-318; a doc_currency claim for STATUS.md:52 · guard: a unit test on the F32 result's it.300 legs asserting >0 disclosed-station rail boardings
  2. Read arm 0 at its horizon with coverage beside every mode, then spend the five paired arms in the decided order (scoring -> choice set -> service quality -> routers -> submodes), one family each. repeat ×2 one per pair
    The only thing that has moved a mode since 11 September is a network change read at it.250 on a run that is not a result; the mechanism ledger's top three movers (F5 router-scorer consistency, E12 headway/reliability, E25 rail bonus) are all built and unrun, and light rail moved the wrong way when the pt access leg became physical.
    change: cities/newcastle/overlays/runs/ (the pair overlays); C.raptor.mode_cost_representation, RUN.replanning.score_msa_representation, RUN.replanning.plan_selector_for_removal, C.time_weights.service_quality_representation · guard: coverage read on BOTH arms of each pair (#174); the reading at it.300, not it.100 (#163)
  3. Make the freight_train row like-for-like: count the emitted closure spans (or state the target on the scheduled basis), read the run's own crossings report, and bring positions/signals-and-crossings.md:34,:49 and motorbike-truck-and-freight.md:38 up to the registry's 44/48.
    313 against 405 is a bookkeeping mismatch the board prints on every run (finding 2), and two position pages still tell the next session the value is 0.
    change: src/analyse/report_mode_ridership.py:251-256; cities/newcastle/build/build_level_crossings.py:478; two position pages · guard: a test that the modelled and target bases name the same closure set; check_doc_currency
  4. One innovation_off_after(first, last, fraction) shared by summarise_run.py:383, run_view.py:318 and the Java formula, with a test at (300, 600, 0.8) -> 540.
    Every warm-started arm (#192 made warm completion a result) gets a wrong relaxation verdict from the Python side while the Java has it right.
    change: src/analyse/iteration_reading.py (new function); the two call sites · guard: the unit test named

Sources: the three collector files under the scratchpad's metrics/, the six lane files under reviews/ and research/, the reference library under cities/newcastle/docs/reports/reference/ (field-survey.json 53 projects + 12 platforms + 68 excluded + 20 calibration methods + 14 gaps; factors.json 94 rows), the board's reader on the result and on arm 0, the targets CSV, the registry and the thirteen position pages.
